value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over East Asia (EAS) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In East Asia (EAS), significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected. CMIP6 models indicate a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. Compared to the recent past (1995–2014), an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is Very likely, and Extremely likely compared to pre-industrial conditions. At higher global warming levels, this increase becomes Virtually certain when compared to both the recent past and pre-industrial conditions. Median increases in 50-year TXx events are projected to be more than 0.5°C, 1°C, and 4°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and median increases in annual TXx are projected to be more than 1.5°C, 2°C, and 4.5°C compared to pre-industrial levels.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Northern Europe (NEU) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Northern Europe (NEU), there is a projected robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall. For a 3°C warmer world, there will be a robust increase in extreme rainfall over 80% of land areas in northern Europe. CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation, with a median increase of more than 15% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 15% in annual Rx1day, Rx5day, and Rx30day compared to pre-industrial. There is high confidence in the intensification of heavy precipitation in NEU.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over West Southern Africa (WSAF) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In West Southern Africa (WSAF), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. Compared to pre-industrial levels, this increase is "Very likely," "Extremely likely," and "Virtually certain" at higher global warming levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. Specifically, compared to the 1°C warming level, there is a median increase of more than 1°C and more than 2.5°C in 50-year TXx events. Compared to pre-industrial levels, there is a median increase of more than 2°C and more than 4.5°C in annual TXx. Mortality-related heat stress levels and deadly temperatures are "very likely" to become more frequent in the future under SSP5-8.5 and RCP4.5/SSP2-4.5 scenarios and for a 2°C global warming (high confidence). Heatwaves and deadly heat stress, along with the frequency of exceeding hot temperature thresholds, will drastically increase by the end of the century under SSP5-8.5 (high confidence). A substantial increase in heatwave magnitude and frequency is projected for most of Africa, including Southern Africa, even with 2°C global warming (high confidence).

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over North Eastern Africa (NEAF) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In North Eastern Africa (NEAF), there is medium confidence in the increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes. An increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected to be virtually certain compared with both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. For the broader African domain, which includes NEAF, a substantial increase in heatwave magnitude and frequency is projected for even 2°C global warming (high confidence). Heatwaves and deadly heat stress, along with the frequency of exceeding hot temperature thresholds (e.g., 35°C), are projected to drastically increase by the end of the century under SSP5-8.5 (high confidence), with NEAF identified as one of the regions expected to experience the largest increases in heat stress.

value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over Northern Central America (NCA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Central America, mean wind speed and wind power potential are projected to increase in most parts (medium confidence). For wind extremes, tropical cyclones are projected to decrease in frequency along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, but with an increased frequency of intense cyclones (medium confidence) for the mid-century or under a 2°C global warming level. For severe wind storms, there is limited evidence and low confidence regarding changes in extratropical cyclones and extreme winds in tropical areas.

In summary, there is limited evidence of current trends in observed wind speed and wind storms in Central and South America. value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Eastern Europe (EEU) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer:
In Eastern Europe (EEU), an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected. This increase is considered very likely compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events.

Specifically, compared to the 1°C warming level, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 0.5°C. At the 1.5°C warming level, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 1.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 2.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. At the 4°C warming level, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 4.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 5.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial.

For almost all AR6 regions, including EEU, it is likely that the intensity and frequency of hot extremes will increase even under 1.5°C global warming. These changes are virtually certain to occur under 4°C global warming.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Tibetan Plateau (TIB) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: Over the Tibetan Plateau (TIB), an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected. Compared with pre-industrial levels, this increase is projected to be "Extremely likely" and "Virtually certain". CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. Median increases in 50-year TXx and TNn events are projected to be more than 0.5°C, more than 1°C, and more than 4°C compared to the 1°C warming level. Median increases in annual TXx and TNn are projected to be more than 1.5°C, more than 2°C, and more than 4.5°C compared to pre-industrial levels. There is "High confidence" for increases in hot temperature extremes.

answer.answer: In North Eastern Africa (NEAF), extreme precipitation intensity is projected to increase (high confidence) for 2°C Global Warming Level (GWL) and higher. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. Specifically, median increases in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level are projected to be more than 4%, more than 8%, and more than 25% at different warming levels. Annual Rx1day and Rx5day are projected to increase by more than 8%, 10%, and 35% compared to pre-industrial levels, while annual Rx30day is projected to increase by more than 6%, 10%, and 30% compared to pre-industrial levels.

answer.answer: CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation in New Zealand. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered Likely (compared with pre-industrial). Daily rainfall extremes are projected to increase in New Zealand with very likely increases. At the 2.0°C global warming level, daily rainfall extremes are projected to increase with medium confidence, while there is low confidence in changes at the 1.5°C warming level.

answer.answer: For Northern Australia, there is low confidence in projected mean wind speeds generally. However, by the end of the 21st century under high emissions scenarios (RCP8.5), there is medium confidence that annual mean wind power will significantly increase in north-eastern Australia. Regarding wind extremes, severe winds are projected to generally increase in north-eastern Australia by the end of the century under RCP8.5 (medium confidence). Additionally, projections for 2074–2100 relative to 1979–2005 under RCP8.5 indicate an increase in 1-in-25-year return period winds in tropical areas of Northern Australia.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over North-Eastern South America (NES) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In North-Eastern South America (NES), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. This increase is considered Likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Very likely (compared with pre-industrial). Further projections indicate it is Very likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Extremely likely (compared with pre-industrial), and even Virtually certain (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Virtually certain (compared with pre-industrial). CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. Specifically, there is a median increase of more than 0.5°C in the 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 1.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. Other projections show a median increase of more than 2.5°C in the 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 4°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. The number of heatwave days is also projected to increase for the intra-Americas region under RCP8.5 for the end of the 21st century.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Central North America (CNA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Central North America (CNA), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase with higher global warming levels. These changes are virtually certain to occur under 4°C global warming. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes (TXx events), with a median increase of more than 4.5°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 5.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. For dangerous heat thresholds (e.g., HI > 41°C), a median increase of 75–150 days per year is projected over much of CNA under the SSP5-8.5 scenario by the end of the century. Climate change is virtually certain to shift temperatures towards warming trends, leading to increases in the magnitude, frequency, duration, and seasonal and spatial extent of heat extremes across North America. Specifically for CNA, the increase in intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected with increasing confidence at higher warming levels: from likely (compared to 1995–2014) to very likely (compared to 1995–2014) and extremely likely (compared to pre-industrial), and ultimately to virtually certain (compared to both 1995–2014 and pre-industrial).

answer.answer: In South-Eastern South America (SES), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase with higher global warming levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of maximum daily temperature (TXx) events. Specifically, a median increase of more than 0.5°C is projected for 50-year TXx and TNn events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 1°C for annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial levels. The number of heatwave days is also projected to increase for the intra-Americas region, which includes SES, by the end of the 21st century under the RCP8.5 scenario. More broadly, at continental scales, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with rising global warming levels. Changes in the intensity of extremes are projected to be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. The number of hot days and hot nights, and the length, frequency, and/or intensity of warm spells or heatwaves, will increase over most land areas with virtual certainty.

answer.answer:
In the Caribbean (CAR), significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected, with the magnitude of these changes increasing with global warming. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events, with median increases of more than 1.5°C, 2°C, and 3.5°C in annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial levels. It is likely that the intensity and frequency of hot temperature extremes will increase in small islands, including CAR. Specifically, the increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is assessed with varying levels of confidence depending on the comparison baseline: Likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014), Very likely (compared with pre-industrial), Very likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014), Extremely likely (compared with pre-industrial), Virtually certain (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014), and Virtually certain (compared with pre-industrial).

Warm spell conditions are projected to occur for up to half the year in CAR at 1.5°C global warming level (GWL), with an additional 70 days at 2°C GWL. Heatwaves are projected to increase in CAR by the mid- and end-century under RCP8.5. An increase of about 30–60 days where the Heat Index (HI) exceeds 41°C is projected by 2041–2060 under SSP5-8.5 relative to 1995–2014, with an additional increase of about 50–100 days by the end of the 21st century for RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Eastern North America (ENA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer:
For Eastern North America (ENA), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes (TXx events). Specifically, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 1.5°C and more than 5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and the median increase in annual TXx is projected to be more than 2.5°C and more than 5.5°C compared to pre-industrial levels.

Regarding the likelihood of changes at different global warming levels:
*   **At 1.5°C global warming:** An increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is Likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Very likely (compared with pre-industrial).
*   **At 2°C global warming:** An increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is Very likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Extremely likely (compared with pre-industrial).
*   **At 4°C global warming:** An increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is Virtually certain (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Virtually certain (compared with pre-industrial).

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over South American Monsoon (SAM) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In the South American Monsoon (SAM) region, CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. There is medium confidence in the intensification of heavy precipitation compared to both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. Specifically, compared to the 1°C warming level, a median increase of more than 10% is projected for 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events. Compared to pre-industrial levels, a median increase of more than 10% is projected for annual Rx1day and Rx5day, and 4% for annual Rx30day. While conflicting projections exist, more weight is given to the CMIP6 results.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Russian Arctic (RAR) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In the Russian Arctic (RAR), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. For 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events, there is a median increase of more than 25% compared to the 1°C warming level, and for annual Rx1day and Rx5day events, there is a median increase of more than 25% compared to pre-industrial levels. Annual Rx30day events are projected to increase by more than 20% compared to pre-industrial levels. The intensification of heavy precipitation is projected as: Likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Very likely (compared with pre-industrial) at 1.5°C global warming; Very likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Extremely likely (compared with pre-industrial) at 2°C global warming; and Virtually certain (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and Virtually certain (compared with pre-industrial) at 4°C global warming. More broadly, the water cycle is projected to intensify in polar regions, leading to more rainfall and more intense precipitation with high confidence.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over East Siberia (ESB) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In East Siberia (ESB), an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected to be Virtually certain compared with both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of maximum daily temperature (TXx) events. Median increases for 50-year TXx events are projected to be more than 0.5°C, 1.5°C, and 4.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 2°C, 2.5°C, and 5.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial levels. An increase in extreme heat durations is expected in all scenarios for East Siberia. Generally, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with higher global warming levels. Changes in the intensity of extremes would be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. In high-latitude regions, changes in the magnitude and intensity of heat extremes are very likely to be more than twice as large as the global surface air temperature (GSAT) warming.

At 4°C warming, intensification of heavy precipitation is very likely (compared with the recent past, 1995–2014) and extremely likely (compared with pre-industrial).

Specifically, for the intensification of heavy precipitation in SCA, there is low confidence compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and low confidence compared with pre-industrial conditions.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western North America (WNA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: For Western North America (WNA), CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. Additional evidence from CMIP5 and RCM simulations also indicates an increase in the intensity of heavy precipitation. Specifically, there is a projected median increase of more than 2% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 6% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 4% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels. More broadly, for North America, the intensity and frequency of extreme precipitation are very likely to increase at higher global warming levels.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Mediterranean (MED) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer:
In the Mediterranean (MED) region, there is a very likely increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes, and significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected. The frequency of heatwaves observed in Europe, including the Mediterranean, has very likely increased in recent decades due to human-induced changes, and these trends are very likely to continue for global warming levels of 1.5°C, 2°C, and 3°C.

CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. Specifically, a median increase of more than 0.5°C in the 50-year TXx and TNn events is projected compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 2°C in annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial levels. Another projection indicates a median increase of more than 3.5°C in the 50-year TXx and TNn events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 5°C in annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial levels.

At higher global warming levels, changes in the intensity of extremes would be at least double at 2°C, and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. Future changes in the intensity of temperature extremes will very likely be proportional to changes in global warming, and up to two to three times larger (high confidence).

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over South-Eastern South America (SES) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In South-Eastern South America (SES), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. Specifically, there is a projected median increase of more than 8% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 20% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 15% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial. Additional evidence from CMIP5 and RCM simulations also indicates an increase in the intensity of heavy precipitation. At global warming levels of 4°C relative to pre-industrial, the increase in frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation is very likely for most AR6 regions, including SES. However, for moderate extreme precipitation, projections are mixed, with increases projected by CORDEXCORE and CMIP5 simulations, while CMIP6 simulations project increases for some regions and decreases for others.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Sahara (SAH) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: At higher global warming levels, the intensification of heavy precipitation in the Sahara (SAH) is projected to be extremely likely compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and virtually certain compared with pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation, with median increases of more than 30% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 40% in annual Rx1day, Rx5day, and Rx30day compared to pre-industrial.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Northern Australia (NAU) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Northern Australia (NAU), significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected, with CMIP6 models indicating a robust increase. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, NAU is projected to experience over 100 more days per year with maximum temperatures exceeding 35°C. Furthermore, there is a strong increase in the projected frequency of exceeding dangerous humid heat thresholds in Northern Australia for RCP8.5 (high confidence).

value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over East Asia (EAS) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: At higher global warming levels, mean surface wind speeds in Asia, including East Asia (EAS), are projected to decline with medium confidence. For wind extremes, tropical cyclones (TCs) in the western Pacific are projected to decrease in frequency but increase in maximum wind intensities. Specifically, simulations for the late 21st century under the RCP8.5 scenario indicate considerably more TCs in the western North Pacific exceeding Category 3 intensity. The intensity of TCs affecting the Japan Islands is projected to increase under the RCP8.5 scenario, while the frequency of TCs affecting the Philippine region and Vietnam is projected to decrease (medium confidence). For extratropical cyclones (ETCs) in the mid- and high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, the number associated with extreme winds is projected to significantly decrease in winter.

answer.answer: CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation over East Siberia (ESB). Specifically, there is a median increase of more than 20% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 20% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 15% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels. This projected increase in heavy precipitation in East Siberia is supported by high confidence, and the intensification is considered "Virtually certain" when compared with both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial conditions.

value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over Caribbean (CAR) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In the Caribbean (CAR) region, projections estimate an increase of up to 0.4 m s–1 (8%) in annual winds under RCP8.5, associated with changes in the North Atlantic Subtropical High and enhanced Caribbean low-level jet during the wet season, and stronger local easterlies in the dry season (low confidence). Regarding wind extremes, tropical cyclone intensity is expected to increase by the end of the century under RCP8.5 due to higher sea surface temperatures, although this can be inhibited by increases in vertical wind shear (medium confidence). Tropical cyclone frequency is projected to decrease, except over the central North Pacific.

answer.answer:
In Central Africa (CAF), there is high confidence that the intensity of extreme precipitation will increase in a future climate at higher global warming levels (GWLs). Specifically, at 1.5°C GWL, CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation, with a median increase of more than 2% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 10% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day, and 8% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered likely compared to pre-industrial levels.

At 2°C GWL, CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation, with a median increase of more than 6% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 10% in annual Rx1day, Rx5day, and Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered very likely compared to pre-industrial levels.

At 4°C GWL, CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation, with a median increase of more than 20% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 30% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day, and 20% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered virtually certain compared to pre-industrial levels.

value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over Southern South America (SSA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Southern South America (SSA), mean wind speeds are projected to decrease in Patagonia. For wind extremes, projections indicate a slight decrease in the number of extratropical cyclones in mid-latitudes (limited evidence, low confidence). Climate models also project a shift and intensification of southern storm tracks, with most effects offshore over the Southern Ocean, and low confidence (low agreement) of significant extreme wind changes over land and coastal areas across the 21st century. Over the Southern Hemisphere, the number of extreme cyclones is projected to increase by at least 20% and up to 50%, with increases in strong cyclones appearing robust across models and seasons, primarily over the southern flank of the storm track.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over South American Monsoon (SAM) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: For the South American Monsoon (SAM) region, an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected to be "Virtually certain" compared with both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models robustly project an increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events (hot extremes). Specifically, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 0.5°C, 1°C, or 2.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 1.5°C, 2°C, or 4.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial levels. Generally, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with higher global warming levels, with changes in the intensity of extremes at least doubling at 2°C and quadrupling at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. The highest increase in the temperature of hottest days is projected in the South American region.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Madagascar (MDG) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Madagascar (MDG), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. For higher global warming levels, compared to the 1°C warming level, a median increase of more than 15% is projected for 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events. Compared to pre-industrial levels, a median increase of more than 15% is projected for annual Rx1day and Rx5day, and more than 6% for annual Rx30day. Additional evidence from CMIP5 and CORDEX simulations also indicates an increase in the intensity of heavy precipitation. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered Extremely likely compared with pre-industrial levels and Very likely compared with the recent past (1995–2014). There is also medium confidence of increase in the intensification of heavy precipitation.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western and Central Europe (WCE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Western and Central Europe (WCE), heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall are projected to increase in both intensity and frequency at higher global warming levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. There is high confidence in an extreme precipitation increase in WCE, with intensification of heavy precipitation being Very likely compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and Extremely likely compared with pre-industrial. These projections are for 2°C Global Warming Level (GWL) and higher, including at 1.5°C, 2°C, and 4°C of global warming. Specifically, CMIP6 models project a median increase of more than 10% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 15% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 10% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over East Southern Africa (ESAF) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In East Southern Africa (ESAF), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of maximum daily temperature (TXx) and minimum daily temperature (TNn) events. Specifically, there is a projected median increase of more than 0.5°C in 50-year TXx and TNn events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 1.5°C in annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial. Further projections indicate a median increase of more than 2.5°C in 50-year TXx and TNn events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 4°C in annual TXx and TNn compared to pre-industrial. Mortality-related heat stress levels and deadly temperatures are very likely to become more frequent for a 2°C global warming, and ESAF is among the regions expected to experience the largest increases in heat stress. Generally, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with higher global warming levels, with changes in the intensity of extremes at least doubling at 2°C and quadrupling at 3°C of global warming compared to changes at 1.5°C.

answer.answer: In Central Australia (CAU), heavy precipitation and pluvial flooding are projected to increase with medium confidence. CMIP6 models project an increase in both the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. Specifically, the intensification of heavy precipitation in CAU is projected as "Likely" with medium confidence when compared to the recent past (1995–2014), and "Very likely" with High confidence when compared to pre-industrial levels. Daily rainfall extremes are also projected to increase over central Australia with medium confidence. A larger increase in global surface temperature leads to a larger increase in extreme precipitation. CMIP6 models project a median increase of more than 10% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 10% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 4% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over South East Asia (SEA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In South East Asia (SEA), hot extremes and extreme heat are projected to increase in both intensity and frequency at higher global warming levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events, with additional evidence from CMIP5 simulations supporting an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes. Extreme heat events are very likely to become more intense and/or more frequent by the end of the 21st century, particularly under higher emissions scenarios such as RCP6.0 and RCP8.5. For example, under SSP5-8.5, the exceedance of the dangerous heat stress 41°C threshold is expected to increase by approximately 250 days in SEA by the end of the century. In contrast, under SSP1-2.6, the increase in exceedance days would be restricted to less than 30 days in many regions, though still higher in SEA.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western and Central Europe (WCE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Western and Central Europe (WCE), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. This increase is considered "Virtually certain" compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of maximum daily temperature (TXx) events. Specifically, there is a median increase of more than 0.5°C, 1.5°C, and 5.5°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 2°C, 3°C, and 6°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial levels. More broadly, for nearly all inhabited regions, including WCE, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with rising global warming levels. Changes in the intensity of extremes are projected to be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C. The number of hot days and hot nights, and the length, frequency, and/or intensity of warm spells or heatwaves, will increase over most land areas (virtually certain). Future changes in the intensity of temperature extremes will very likely be proportional to changes in global warming, and up to two to three times larger (high confidence).

For wind extremes, there is medium confidence of a general decrease in the number of extratropical cyclones producing high wind speeds in North America. Specifically, CMIP5 models project a significant decrease in the number of extratropical cyclones (ETCs) associated with extreme winds in the mid- and high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere in winter, with a larger projected decrease over the Atlantic by the end of the century. For severe wind storms, there is disagreement between global- and regional-model change projections in eastern Canada. Generally, tropical cyclones, severe wind, and dust storms in North America are shifting towards more extreme characteristics, with a stronger signal towards heightened intensity than increased frequency, though specific regional patterns remain more uncertain (medium confidence).

Pu and Ginoux (2017) project about five more dusty days in spring and summer in the southern Great Plains under RCP8.5 at the end of the century, while dusty days decrease in northern regions where mean precipitation tends towards wetter conditions. Tropical cyclones, severe wind and dust storms in North America are shifting towards more extreme characteristics, with a stronger signal towards heightened intensity than increased frequency, although specific regional patterns are more uncertain ( medium confidence). Mean wind speed and wind power potential are projected to decrease in Western North America (medium confidence) with differences between global and regional models lending low confidence elsewhere.

answer.answer: For North America, which includes Eastern North America (ENA), the intensity and frequency of extreme precipitation are very likely to increase at higher global warming levels. Generally, heavy precipitation will become more frequent and more intense with additional global warming across all AR6 regions, including ENA. Specifically, at global warming levels of 4°C relative to pre-industrial levels, very rare heavy precipitation events (e.g., one in 10 or more years) would become more frequent and more intense than in the recent past (virtually certain). For global warming levels above 2°C, very rare heavy precipitation events are projected to be more frequent and more intense over nearly all AR6 regions (virtually certain).

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over South-Western South America (SWS) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In South-Western South America (SWS), significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected, with CMIP6 models indicating a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events. This increase in intensity and frequency of hot extremes is considered "Virtually certain" compared to both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. At higher global warming levels, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase. Specifically, changes in the intensity of extremes would be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming. The number of hot days and hot nights, and the length, frequency, and/or intensity of warm spells or heatwaves, will increase over most land areas (virtually certain), with the highest increase of temperature of hottest days projected in the South American region. For SWS, CMIP6 models project median increases in 50-year TXx events of more than 0.5°C compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 1.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. Other projections show median increases of more than 1°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level and more than 2.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial, or more than 3°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level and more than 4.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial.

answer.answer: CMIP6 models project an increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation over Southern Australia (SAU). Specifically, a median increase of more than 10% is projected for 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 8% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 4% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial. However, there is low confidence in the intensification of heavy precipitation in SAU compared with the recent past (1995–2014) and compared with pre-industrial. For daily rainfall extremes, there is medium confidence on increases over Southern Australia.

Daily and interannual wind variability is also projected to increase in Northern Europe under RCP8.5 (low confidence).

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over Russian Far East (RFE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In the Russian Far East (RFE), an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is projected with medium confidence. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events (hot extremes). An increase in extreme heat durations is expected in all scenarios. Compared to the 1°C warming level, CMIP6 models project median increases in 50-year TXx events of more than 0.5°C, more than 1°C, and more than 4.5°C. Compared to pre-industrial levels, median increases in annual TXx are projected to be more than 1.5°C, more than 2.5°C, and more than 5°C.

answer.answer: In Southern Australia (SAU), the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected to increase. This increase is considered Virtually certain when compared with both the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels. Compared to the 1°C warming level, the median increase in 50-year TXx events is projected to be more than 2°C. When compared to pre-industrial levels, the median increase in annual TXx is projected to be more than 2.5°C.

answer.answer: Projections indicate a decrease in severe winds in some parts of Southern Australia (SAU) by the end of the century under the RCP8.5 scenario, with medium confidence. However, there is low confidence in projected mean wind speeds and wind power potential in Australasia, with no specific projection for Southern Australia.

In New Zealand, mean wind patterns are projected to become more north-easterly in summer, and westerlies to become more intense in winter (low confidence), in agreement with the strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere storm tracks (Section 4.5.1). Severe wind storm: There is generally low confidence in observed changes in extreme winds and extratropical storms in Australasia (Section 11.7.2). Elsewhere trends are diverse and vary across simulations with low agreement. Projections of changes in the 1-in-25-year return period winds (based on annual maxima) for 2074–2100 relative to 1979–2005 for RCP8.5 show an increase in tropical areas of Northern Australia (Kumar et al., 2015). answer.answer: There is low confidence in the projected change in the magnitude of very heavy precipitation days in the Caribbean (CAR) across different global warming levels. The direction of change in extreme precipitation in the Pacific, which includes parts of the Caribbean, varies by season (low confidence). One projection indicates a decrease in days with intense rainfall in the Caribbean under 2°C global warming by the 2050s.

answer.answer: In South Asia (SAS), there is high confidence that heavy precipitation is projected to intensify. CMIP6 models project a robust increase in both the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. A half-degree difference in warming between 1.5°C and 2.0°C can lead to a detectable increase in extreme precipitation over South Asia. Specifically, CMIP6 models project a median increase of more than 25% in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 30% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 25% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial levels.

value.question: How are hot extremes and extreme heat projected to change in intensity and frequency over West Siberia (WSB) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In West Siberia (WSB), significant increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes are projected. CMIP6 models indicate a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of TXx events, and an increase in extreme heat durations is expected across all scenarios. Compared to the recent past (1995–2014) and pre-industrial levels, an increase in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes is Virtually certain. More specifically, compared to pre-industrial, this increase is Extremely likely. CMIP6 models project a median increase of more than 1°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 2.5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. Other projections from CMIP6 models indicate a median increase of more than 4°C in 50-year TXx events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 5°C in annual TXx compared to pre-industrial. Generally, for high-latitude regions like West Siberia, changes in extreme metrics are very likely to be more than the global surface air temperature (GSAT) warming. At a global and continental scale, the frequency and intensity of hot extremes will continue to increase with higher global warming levels; changes in the intensity of extremes would be at least double at 2°C and quadruple at 3°C of global warming, compared to changes at 1.5°C of global warming.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Western Africa (WAF) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In Western Africa (WAF), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. At higher global warming levels, the projected increases are more significant. For instance, compared to the 1°C warming level, the median increase in 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events is projected to be more than 4% at 2°C warming, and more than 25% at 4°C warming. Annual Rx1day and Rx5day events are projected to increase by more than 15% at 2°C warming and more than 30% at 4°C warming compared to pre-industrial levels. There is high confidence that the intensity of extreme precipitation will increase in a future climate in West Africa. The intensification of heavy precipitation is considered "Likely" compared with pre-industrial levels at 2°C warming, and "Virtually certain" at 4°C warming.

value.question: How are mean wind speed and wind extremes projected to change in intensity and frequency over West Central Asia (WCA) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In West Central Asia (WCA), mean wind speeds are projected to decrease with medium confidence in future climate scenarios. For wind extremes, there is low confidence that extra-tropical cyclones will decline in number (frequency) in future climate scenarios over WCA. There is limited evidence for projection of changes in other severe winds.

value.question: How are heavy precipitation and extreme rainfall projected to change in intensity and frequency over Russian Far East (RFE) at higher global warming levels?

answer.answer: In the Russian Far East (RFE), CMIP6 models project a robust increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy precipitation. There is medium confidence in the intensification of heavy precipitation, and models consistently project an increase in heavy precipitation with high confidence. Specifically, CMIP6 models project a median increase of more than 25% in the 50-year Rx1day and Rx5day events compared to the 1°C warming level, and more than 25% in annual Rx1day and Rx5day and 20% in annual Rx30day compared to pre-industrial. The CMIP6 multi-model median also projects an increase in the 10- and 50-year return values of Rx1day and Rx5day at a rate between 5% and 6% per 1°C of near-surface global mean warming.
